newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean stocks plunge on oversupply, probe fears.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean stocks plunge on oversupply, probe fears.

text.p: South Korean shares fell to a three-year low for the second straight day on Tuesday, weighed down by fears of new shares flooding the market and concerns over the government's anti-corruption crusade.
The composite stock index, down nearly 26 percent from a year high in May, lost 13.77 points or 1.84 percent on Tuesday to close at 733.65.
The index's slide past technical support at 750 on Monday exacerbated the market's already bearish tone, prompting brisk selling on Tuesday, brokers and analysts said.
"The 750 level was seen as strong support," said market analyst Steven Lee of Shinyoung Securities. "Once that line was broken, people didn't know where it would stop."

Brokers said loans for margin trading are at a record high of around three trillion won ($3.63 billion) while customer deposits have fallen to 2.5 trillion won. Between 500-900 billion won in loans will have to be repaid just this month.
"Everyone knew about the margin loans and the oversupply of shares. It's now a psychological issue. People are really afraid to hold shares," said Choi Tae-hwan, head of sales at KLB Securities.
New stock supply valued at over 1.1 trillion won will come into the market in November, broking analysts said.
This includes 500 billion won of Korea Telecom shares to be sold by the government, about 240 billion won of new rights issues and almost 450 billion won of initial public offerings.
Investors also fear government probes into illicit share trading which analysts said could cause some major investors to pull money out of the market, brokers said.
The market was also focused on political concerns.
President Kim Young-sam has staked his political reputation on fighting corruption, but was recently embarrassed by the arrest of a former defense minister for accepting bribes.
Prosecutors have said investigations into the former defence minister would cover all levels of civil servants and last through to the end of Kim's term in 1998.

"If we had an optimistic outlook on the market, none of these things would matter," said Stephen Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities. "But right now, any little piece of bad news is enough to knock down investors."
He blamed the market's downward spiral on fundamental economic issues, such as South Korea's widening trade deficit.
"I think a stabilised trade account will put a floor on the market's drop," Marvin said, adding that the market was likely to fall below 700 before a significant turnaround.
The trade deficit soared to $1.57 billion in October, compared to a $207 million shortfall a year earlier.
Finance ministry officials denied local media reports that the ministry was planning a package of steps to boost the sagging stock market, including halting new rights issues.
However, last week the government said it would delay privatisation of four big state-run corporations.
"Given the current depression of the stock market, it will be difficult to sell a large amount of government stock," Suh Seung-gil, director of the finance ministry's treasury bureau, said last week.

Korea Gas Corp and Korea Heavy Industries & Construction Corp had originally been set to be privatised in 1995, while Korea Tobacco & Ginseng Corp -- the state liquour and cigarette monopoly -- was to be handed over to the private sector in 1998.
No new timetables were given.
But the auction of 4.6 percent, or 13.3 million shares of Korea Telecom on November 11-12 will continue as planned. ($1 = 826 won)
